title: Zheng He's Treasure Fleets

cards.h: China sent the biggest fleet in the world, then stopped
cards.b:
In 1405, a fleet of hundreds of ships, carrying nearly 28,000 men, left Nanjing for the Indian Ocean. It was commanded by a eunuch admiral from a Muslim family in Yunnan.

Sixty years before Columbus and Vasco da Gama, China ruled the waves. Then it went home.

Zheng He was born Ma He in 1371 in Yunnan. As a boy he was captured by Ming forces, made a eunuch and served the prince who became the Yongle Emperor (reigned 1402-1424).

Yongle wanted to show China's glory, win tribute from foreign rulers, and perhaps look for his rival, the vanished previous emperor.

The fleets visited Vietnam, Java, Sumatra, Sri Lanka, India, Hormuz, Aden and the East African coast, perhaps reaching Mecca by some members. The treasure ships were huge, though old claims of about 120 metres long are debated; many scholars think they were smaller.

In 1414 a ruler from Bengal sent a giraffe to China (some say it was brought later from Africa). Courtiers called it a qilin, a lucky mythical beast, and celebrated.

The fleet also took silk and porcelain, and returned with spices, gems and ambassadors.

After Yongle died, Confucian officials thought the voyages too costly. Money was needed to fight the Mongols and to rebuild the capital at Beijing. The new emperor Xuande ended the voyages after 1433.

A story says officials burned the records. Historians now doubt it; the documents may simply have been lost or ignored.
China sailed for prestige, with a vast navy. Europeans sailed for profit and kept coming.

Myth: the 2002 book 1421: The Year China Discovered the World by Gavin Menzies claimed the Chinese reached America, and more.Fact: historians reject it. No Chinese records, no archaeology and no maps support it. It sold well but is considered fantasy.

What is true: his fleet really was spectacular, and it was real naval power.

Five things to remember

  1. Zheng He led seven voyages (1405-1433).
  2. He served the Yongle emperor.
  3. The fleets were huge for their time.
  4. Costs and politics ended the voyages.
  5. Calicut was a key stop; da Gama came 65 years later.

Think about it

  • Is power measured by what you can do, or what you choose to do?
  • Why did Europeans keep going where China stopped?
